title: Type Conversion and Coercion
learning_outcomes: Explain the role of type conversion and coercion and identify its main inputs, outputs or constraints.
Apply implicit coercion in a minimal example and state the expected result before checking it.
Test one relevant edge, missing or failure case and describe a limitation of the result.

content.intro: Type Conversion and Coercion is part of Data Types, Values, and Basic Objects. Start with implicit coercion and connect it to the worked example and expected result.
content.why_it_matters: R values have storage types and sometimes class-specific behavior; inspect both before converting or calculating.

content_blocks.title: Why this matters
content_blocks.text: R values have storage types and sometimes class-specific behavior; inspect both before converting or calculating. The example is intentionally small so you can predict its result before checking it in a local R session.

items.title: Implicit Coercion
items.text: Explain implicit coercion in the context of type conversion and coercion, connect it to the example, and verify one expected result or edge case.

items.text: Use explicit conversion with as.*() functions to make input, output and scope explicit, then test both a typical call and one edge case.

items.title: Common Coercion Errors
items.text: For common coercion errors, include a failing or boundary case and explain how it should be detected without silently losing information.

content_blocks.title: Work through it
content_blocks.text: Compare the input type with the returned type, then test an empty or missing value. Change one input or condition at a time, compare the observed result with your prediction, and write down one limitation.

content_blocks.title: R example: Type Conversion and Coercion
content_blocks.code:
# Lesson 23: Type Conversion and Coercion
example_values <- c(4, NA, 6)
is.na(example_values)

content_blocks.limitations: Inspect type and missingness explicitly before converting or summarizing values. Verify the snippet and expected output with the supported R and package versions before publishing.

content_blocks.title: Common pitfall
content_blocks.text: Do not treat a syntactically plausible example as proof of correctness. For type conversion and coercion, check the input type, missing/empty cases, output shape, and domain assumptions.

common_mistakes.problem: Using an example without checking its inputs or output shape.
common_mistakes.why: R can coerce types, propagate missing values or simplify results unexpectedly.
common_mistakes.fix: Inspect with str(), class(), typeof(), length() or dim() and add a direct check.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating a demonstration as proof that every edge case works.
common_mistakes.why: Empty input, missing values, dependencies and version differences can change behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Test a normal case and a boundary/failure case in a clean local R session.

common_mistakes.why: The conclusion depends on data provenance, transformations and assumptions.
common_mistakes.fix: Record input source, cleaning choices and known limitations beside the result.
